note: Vol. I No. 15, and the richest single issue of the month. It carries the Board of Trustees' order for the first built sidewalk on South Water Street — ten feet wide, gravel or brick, two-inch oak curbing, from the United States reservation to Randolph — and, three columns away, the bill of oak timber for the piers of the Chicago Harbor. Beside those two pieces of public works stand twelve storefronts, five of them placed against a named corner or counted in doors off a named building, a livery stable at the Point, a smoke house, an infant school house, a district school house, a burying ground eroding into the lake, and a post-office letter list on page 4 that no previous sweep had found because the segmenter cut its heading in half.

claims.notes: THE STREET EDGE, ORDERED INTO EXISTENCE, WITH ITS DIMENSIONS. This is the town ordering the first built sidewalk on South Water Street and it states four things a reconstruction can use directly: the RUN (every lot from the United States reservation east to Randolph Street), the WIDTH (ten feet), the MATERIAL (gravelled OR brick, the owner's choice), and the EDGE (two-inch oak curbing). The grade is not stated as a number and is not guessed at here: it is 'the pitch of the Town surveyor', i.e. deferred to an officer, so the ordinance fixes the plan and not the profile. THE DATE IS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE BY SIXTEEN MONTHS and the deadline it sets — 'on or before the first day of July next', 1 July 1834 — is a year to the day before the scene. The ordinance is what was ORDERED; whether the walks were built is a separate question this claim does not answer, and the trustees' fallback clause (they will build it at the owners' expense) is evidence they expected some owners not to. The meeting itself places the board: it sat in Dexter Graves's house, not in a public building, which is what a town with no town hall does.

claims.notes: THE PIERS ARE UNDER CONSTRUCTION AND THIS IS THEIR BILL OF TIMBER. A reconstruction that wants to know what the 1834 harbour works were MADE of has it here in numbers: 10,000 feet of hewn oak squared a full foot on the side, in equal thirds of 30-, 25- and 20-foot logs; 350 round tie logs 24 feet long squaring about 11 inches; and 50 round white-oak PILES 25 feet long squaring at least 12 inches at the small end. Poplar and soft wood are bought only to float the oak rafts down, which is why they are specified loose. The delivery clause dates the work: one third at the Piers by 15 April 1834 and the rest inside that month, so the piers were being built out through the spring of 1834, fifteen months before the scene date. claims.notes: WHERE THE TOWN'S BUILDING MATERIAL CAME FROM, IN A SENTENCE: 'lumber from the Lake, lath, shingles, red cedar posts'. Carver is not a sawyer — he is the importer, and the supply chain is named end to end: agents at St. Joseph and Michigan City on the Michigan shore forward to him, and he has CHARTERED THE SCHOONER POST BOY for the season's first two trips so as to land the first cargo of the year. That is the fabric of 1834 Chicago arriving by water because there was no other way for it to arrive. No address is given for his store — 'at his Store' is all the notice says — so the placement is recorded as `none` rather than guessed at, which is the honest value here. THE COLONEL KEEPS HIS TITLE (T-1040). This reading normalized the signature 'Col. Samuel Miller' to 'Samuel Miller', and the 25 February impression of the SAME advertisement (chicago_democrat_1834_02_25 c003) kept it — so one man in one notice printed twice stood in the gazetteer as two persons, `person_samuel_miller` and `person_col_samuel_miller`. The title is restored here because the page sets it, because this corpus keeps a printed title in a normalized name elsewhere ('Col. G. S. Hubbard', 'Capt. N. Leonard', 'Dr. John T. Temple'), and because dropping it is what handed the reading to a different man: the town's own lists carry a Samuel Miller of Chicago, and an identical normalized name is the whole of merge rule M1.

THE NAMES ARE CUT ON THEIR LEFT EDGE, which is the opposite damage to January's: the crop has taken the forenames, so 'as Bennett' and 'ell Baldwin' are minted as the fragments they are, with `[…]` marking the cut, and NOT completed into the Thomas Bennett and Russell Baldwin who stand in the 1 January list — a completion that would look right and prove nothing. WHICH RETURN THIS IS CANNOT BE READ. The date line survives only as '34.', and the name set is neither the January list nor a subset of it: Atkins, Benton, Conger, Carrier, Crisey and Delano are new here, while much of January's list is absent. A quarterly return of 1 March 1834 is the obvious candidate and is NOT asserted, because the paper's own words for it are gone. THE COUNT IS A FLOOR, and a low one: eighteen names from this half-column, against the ninety-seven of 1834-01-28. See claim c025 for the hand count of the whole list. MONTGOMERY' whole in the 1834-01-28 printing, which the corpus already carries. The initial is therefore W. NO PERSON IS MINTED FROM THIS CLAIM, because this column carries no legible signature. The lines cited interleave with the letter list of claim c025, which shares this crop — the same lines carry both, and each claim names only what its own text says. THE SIGNATURE IS LOTON W. MONTGOMERY'S, AND THE SHOEMAKING IS NOT THE AUCTIONEER'S (T-1040). This is ONE standing advertisement — 'Boot & Shoe Making. Cohen's Store …', the same setting word for word under a dateline of Chicago, December 1833 — and the Democrat runs it from 17 December 1833 through at least 8 April 1834. claims.notes: A NAMED HOUSE — THE MAN TRAP — WITH A DOOR AND A VIEW. This is the only trading premises in the month that has a NAME of its own rather than a proprietor's, and the name is a joke about what it does to the passer-by. It is placed opposite R. A. Kinzie's store, which is a second Chicago storefront used as an anchor (Kinzie advertises whiskey and Ohio flour in all three March issues), and it sells fresh bread, cakes, pastry and liquors of every description — so it is a bakery, a confectioner's and a drinking house at once, which is what a frontier town supports instead of three separate trades. THE ADDRESS TO THE READER IS EVIDENCE OF WHO WAS IN THE STREET: 'Hoosiers, Wolverines, Suckers, behold!' names Indianans, Michiganders and Illinoisans, and the subscribers then thank 'their patrons, the Pottawatamies' — the Potawatomi, who by treaty of September 1833 were to be removed west but were still in and around the town through 1835, and who are here addressed as CUSTOMERS by a Chicago baker. That is worth more to a reconstruction of the street than the bread is. AND IT IS ALREADY OVER: this same issue carries John Wellmaker's own notice that the business is closed (claim c011), and on 25 March the partnership is formally dissolved. A standing advertisement outlives the shop it advertises, which is precisely why ruling 3's veto is carried by a claim and not by a date.

claims.notes: THE NEWSPAPER'S OWN ADDRESS, AND IT IS A CORNER: South Water and Clark. The Democrat's terms notice states where the paper is printed, which places a PRINTING OFFICE — press, cases, and a room big enough for both — at the corner of South Water and Clark Streets in March 1834. Two things make this claim worth more than a normal storefront. First, the office is not a shop and so is a different KIND of building on a street this project is trying to populate. Second, W. Kimball's 'New Store on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' (1834-03-18, claim c015 there) is on the same corner by the same words, so two documented occupants stand at one crossing without either saying which side of it — which is the honest limit of what a corner address gives you, and is recorded rather than resolved. Claims c026 and c027 of this issue are the two crops the segmenter cut from page 4's second printed column, and an advertisement stands down the middle of that column: between them they carry 78 of the return's 170 printed lines. T-0424 read the whole column at the scan and set every line down in `data/research/newspapers/letter_list_1834_01_01_printed.json`; T-1010 counted what each line reaches and found 54 that reach nothing at all — not refused by any rule, merely never read into a claim. This claim is those 54 lines, in printed order, from the same impression, the same page and the same column as the crops beside it. It is a LIFT of a reading already made and gated, not a second reading: `as_printed` is the type's own setting, unamended, and each entity's `normalized` is identical to it because at the image there is nothing left to resolve. RULING 1 APPLIES, as it does to c026 and c027: this is Chicago's own office, so a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged `letter_list_only` — and the minting pass's own refusals decide which of them the town keeps.
